common_name: Applejack Rose (Fragrant Deep Pink Cold-Hardy Own-Root Shrub Rose)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container roses in late winter or early spring in slightly acidic, well-amended, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Applejack is a Griffith Buck-bred rose from Iowa State University, prized for extreme cold hardiness on its own roots.

directions: Plant in slightly acidic, well-amended, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Applejack bears large, semi-double, deep pink flowers with prominent golden stamens and a strong, sweet fragrance reminiscent of apples, on a tall, vigorous, own-root shrub bred at Iowa State University by Griffith Buck specifically to survive harsh Midwestern winters without winter protection. It blooms in a heavy spring flush with lighter repeat bloom through summer, and its large size and arching canes suit it to an informal hedge or large border planting. Because it grows on its own roots rather than being grafted, winter dieback simply regrows true to type. It needs far less spray intervention than most hybrid teas, tolerating black spot and other diseases with only moderate care.
sources: Iowa State University — Griffith Buck Rose Introductions

common_name: Prairie Star Rose (Cream-Pink Blend Cold-Hardy Own-Root Shrub Rose)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container roses in late winter or early spring in slightly acidic, well-amended, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Prairie Star is a Griffith Buck-bred rose from Iowa State University, prized for cold hardiness on its own roots.

directions: Plant in slightly acidic, well-amended, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Prairie Star bears large, semi-double blooms in a soft blend of cream and pale pink with a light, sweet fragrance, on a compact, well-branched, own-root shrub bred at Iowa State University by Griffith Buck for reliable performance through harsh Midwestern winters without winter protection. It blooms in a heavy spring flush with continued lighter bloom through summer. Because it grows on its own roots, winter dieback simply regrows true to type rather than reverting to rootstock. It needs far less spray intervention than most hybrid teas, tolerating black spot and other common rose diseases with only moderate care.
sources: Iowa State University — Griffith Buck Rose Introductions

common_name: Country Dancer Rose (Rose-Red Cold-Hardy Own-Root Shrub Rose)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container roses in late winter or early spring in slightly acidic, well-amended, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Country Dancer is a Griffith Buck-bred rose from Iowa State University, prized for cold hardiness on its own roots.

directions: Plant in slightly acidic, well-amended, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Country Dancer bears double, rose-red blooms with a light, sweet fragrance on a compact, bushy, own-root shrub bred at Iowa State University by Griffith Buck for reliable performance through harsh Midwestern winters without winter protection. It reblooms through the growing season with only moderate care, tolerating black spot and other common rose diseases far better than older hybrid teas. Because it grows on its own roots, any winter dieback simply regrows true to type rather than reverting to rootstock. Deadhead spent blooms to encourage continued flowering, and prune moderately in late winter to shape the plant.
sources: Iowa State University — Griffith Buck Rose Introductions

common_name: Carefree Delight Rose (Pink with White Eye Landscape Shrub Rose)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container roses in late winter or early spring in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Carefree Delight is a low-maintenance landscape shrub rose bred by Meilland for disease resistance and nonstop bloom.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Carefree Delight is a low-maintenance landscape shrub rose bred by the French Meilland rose house, bearing single, five-petaled, bright pink flowers with a distinct white eye at the center, produced in large clusters almost continuously from late spring through frost with essentially no deadheading required. Its dense, mounding, self-cleaning habit and strong resistance to black spot and powdery mildew have made it a favorite for commercial and residential landscaping where a tough, reliable flowering shrub is wanted with minimal spray or maintenance. Small orange-red hips follow the flowers into fall, adding a further season of interest and a food source for birds. It requires only an annual shaping prune in late winter to stay tidy.
